subject: Human Performance
description: SACAA PPL Human Performance question bank covering respiration and circulation, hypoxia, hyperventilation, vision, hearing, spatial disorientation, vestibular system, fatigue, stress, information processing, decision making, and fitness to fly.

questions.question: A decrease in the amount of haemoglobin in the red blood cells leads to a condition called:-
questions.explanation: Anaemia is a condition where there is a decrease in the amount of haemoglobin in the red blood cells, or a decrease in the number of red blood cells. Haemoglobin is the protein that carries oxygen. Anaemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and can lead to anaemic hypoxia.

questions.question: The volume of oxygen in the atmosphere is approximately:-
questions.explanation: The atmosphere is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases (argon, carbon dioxide, etc.). This proportion remains constant at all altitudes — it is the partial pressure of oxygen that decreases with altitude, not the percentage.

questions.question: The breathing rate is determined by:-

options.text: the level of carbon dioxide in the blood
the amount of oxygen required by the body

questions.explanation: The breathing rate is primarily controlled by the level of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the blood, detected by chemoreceptors in the brain stem. When CO₂ levels rise, the breathing rate increases to expel the excess CO₂. This is why hyperventilation (over-breathing) reduces CO₂ and disrupts the breathing control mechanism.

questions.question: Blood is pumped around the body by the:-
questions.explanation: The left ventricle is the main pumping chamber that pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the entire body (systemic circulation). The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation). The atria are receiving chambers. The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall because it must generate the highest pressure.

questions.question: Oxygen rich blood:-

options.text: is found in the right ventricle

questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood is bright red due to oxyhaemoglobin (haemoglobin bound to oxygen). Deoxygenated blood is darker red (appears bluish through the skin). Oxygenated blood is found in the left side of the heart (left atrium and left ventricle) and in the arteries (except the pulmonary artery).

questions.question: The pumping or discharge chambers of the heart are:-

options.text: the left ventricle and the right ventricle
the left atrium and the right atrium
the left atrium and the left ventricle
the right atrium and the right ventricle

questions.explanation: The ventricles are the pumping (discharge) chambers of the heart. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the body; the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The atria are the receiving chambers that collect blood returning to the heart.

questions.question: When measuring blood pressure the lowest reading obtained is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is expressed as systolic/diastolic (e.g., 120/80 mmHg). Systolic is the higher reading (pressure when the heart contracts). Diastolic is the lower reading (pressure when the heart relaxes between beats). High blood pressure (hypertension) increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

questions.question: A person suffering from sustained low blood pressure may experience:-
questions.explanation: Low blood pressure (hypotension) reduces blood flow to the brain, causing dizziness, light-headedness, or fainting (syncope). This can be caused by dehydration, prolonged standing, blood loss, or certain medications. In aviation, fainting is extremely dangerous as it results in loss of aircraft control.

questions.question: In terms of the Gas laws, Dalton's Law states that:-

options.text: the total pressure of a gas mixture is equal to the sum of its partial pressures
the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to pressure

questions.explanation: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures: the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each individual gas. At sea level, total pressure is 1013 hPa; oxygen's partial pressure is 21% × 1013 = 213 hPa. At altitude, total pressure decreases, so oxygen's partial pressure also decreases, leading to hypoxia.

questions.question: A pilot's susceptibility to hypoxia:-

options.text: increases with the consumption of alcohol, drugs, and tobacco
is not affected by lifestyle factors

questions.explanation: Alcohol, drugs, and tobacco all increase susceptibility to hypoxia. Alcohol impairs the brain's ability to use oxygen. Carbon monoxide from tobacco binds to haemoglobin 200-300 times more readily than oxygen, reducing oxygen-carrying capacity. Certain medications can also impair oxygen utilisation. A smoker's effective altitude is approximately 5000 ft higher than actual altitude.

questions.question: Hypoxic hypoxia occurs as a result of:-

options.text: an insufficient partial pressure of oxygen

questions.explanation: Hypoxic hypoxia is caused by insufficient partial pressure of oxygen in the inspired air — the most common type in aviation, occurring at altitude. The four types of hypoxia are: (1) Hypoxic — low oxygen pressure (altitude), (2) Anaemic — reduced haemoglobin (anaemia, CO poisoning), (3) Stagnant — poor circulation, (4) Histotoxic — cells cannot use oxygen (alcohol, drugs).

questions.question: The time of useful consciousness is:-

options.text: the time available to recognise the onset of hypoxia and take corrective action
the total time a pilot can fly without rest
the time before a pilot falls asleep

questions.explanation: The Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) is the period from when oxygen supply is interrupted until the pilot can no longer take effective corrective action. TUC decreases rapidly with altitude: at 25,000 ft it is 3-5 minutes; at 35,000 ft it is 30-60 seconds; at 40,000 ft it is 15-20 seconds. Physical activity reduces TUC.

questions.question: In order to treat hyperventilation:-

options.text: breathing into a paper bag will increase the body's level of carbon dioxide which will return the breathing rate to normal

questions.explanation: Hyperventilation is over-breathing that washes out too much CO₂ from the blood. Treatment: (1) Consciously slow the breathing rate, (2) Breathe into a paper bag to re-inhale CO₂, (3) Talk or sing (regulates breathing). Symptoms include tingling, dizziness, light-headedness, and muscle spasms. It can be triggered by anxiety, stress, or pain.

questions.question: Anaemic hypoxia may be caused by:-

options.text: a reduction in the amount of circulating haemoglobin

questions.explanation: Anaemic hypoxia results from a reduction in the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. Causes include: anaemia (low haemoglobin), carbon monoxide poisoning (CO binds to haemoglobin, blocking oxygen), blood loss, and blood donation. After blood donation, a pilot should not fly for at least 72 hours.

questions.question: Prevention of hypoxia in a non-pressurised aircraft is best achieved by:-

options.text: remaining at an altitude which will provide an adequate oxygen pressure gradient

questions.explanation: The best prevention of hypoxia in unpressurised aircraft is to fly at altitudes where the oxygen partial pressure is sufficient. Below 10,000 ft, most healthy individuals can function normally. Above 10,000 ft, supplemental oxygen should be used. Regulations typically require oxygen above 12,500 ft for crew and above 14,000 ft for passengers.

questions.question: A consequence of hyperventilation is that there will be:-

options.text: a shortage of carbon dioxide in the blood
too much oxygen in the blood
a shortage of oxygen in the blood
too much carbon dioxide in the blood

questions.explanation: Hyperventilation (over-breathing) causes excessive loss of carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the blood. This raises blood pH (respiratory alkalosis), causing: tingling in extremities, dizziness, visual disturbances, muscle spasms, and eventually unconsciousness. The symptoms can mimic hypoxia, making diagnosis difficult at altitude.

questions.question: Whilst using oxygen masks passengers should be cautioned against breathing rapidly or deeply in order to avoid:-
questions.explanation: When using supplemental oxygen, passengers may tend to breathe rapidly or deeply due to anxiety. This can cause hyperventilation (excessive loss of CO₂), producing symptoms that may be confused with hypoxia. Passengers should be briefed to breathe normally and calmly when using oxygen masks.

questions.question: According to Dalton's Law:-

options.text: the proportion of oxygen remains at 21% throughout the atmosphere
the amount of oxygen in each breath remains constant at any altitude

questions.explanation: Dalton's Law confirms that the proportion (percentage) of each gas in a mixture remains constant regardless of total pressure. Oxygen is always 21% of the atmosphere at any altitude. However, as total atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen decreases proportionally, reducing the amount of oxygen available per breath.

questions.question: As altitude is gained the amount of oxygen in each breath:-
questions.explanation: While the percentage of oxygen remains at 21%, the actual amount (mass) of oxygen in each breath decreases with altitude because the air is less dense. At 18,000 ft, atmospheric pressure is approximately half that at sea level, so each breath contains roughly half the oxygen molecules compared to sea level.

questions.question: The 'time of useful consciousness' at 25,000 ft following rapid decompression is approximately:-
questions.explanation: At 25,000 ft following rapid decompression, the TUC is approximately 2-3 minutes (reduced from 3-5 minutes at gradual onset because rapid decompression causes immediate oxygen loss from the lungs). Rapid decompression halves the normal TUC. The pilot must immediately don an oxygen mask and initiate an emergency descent.

questions.question: The amount of light which enters the eye is controlled by the:-
questions.explanation: The iris is the coloured part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil (the opening). In bright light, the iris constricts the pupil to reduce light entry. In dim light, the iris dilates the pupil to allow more light in. This process is called the pupillary reflex and is automatic.

questions.question: In order to correct long sightedness (hypermetropia):-
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia (long/far sightedness) occurs when the eyeball is too short or the lens too flat — the image focuses behind the retina. A convex (converging) lens corrects this by bending light rays inward before they enter the eye. Myopia (short sightedness) is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.

questions.question: With reference to the eye, the rods:-

options.text: are used for peripheral vision and night vision

questions.explanation: Rods are photoreceptor cells in the retina that are sensitive to low light levels and are responsible for peripheral (side) vision and night vision. They cannot detect colour. Rods are concentrated around the periphery of the retina. Cones are concentrated in the fovea (centre) and are responsible for colour vision and sharp detail in bright light.

questions.question: Vision in low levels of illumination or at night is dependent upon:-
questions.explanation: Night vision depends on the rod cells in the retina. Rods are very sensitive to low light levels but cannot distinguish colour (which is why we see in shades of grey at night). Rods require up to 30 minutes to fully adapt to darkness (dark adaptation). Exposure to bright light destroys dark adaptation.

questions.question: Good night vision is best achieved by:-

options.text: looking to the side of the object in order to focus the image on the rods

questions.explanation: At night, looking slightly to the side of an object (off-centre viewing) places the image on the peripheral retina where rods are concentrated, rather than on the fovea (which has mainly cones and a 'blind spot' for dim light). Scan the area using short eye movements rather than staring at one point.

questions.question: In order to correct short sightedness (myopia):-
questions.explanation: Myopia (short/near sightedness) occurs when the eyeball is too long or the lens too curved — the image focuses in front of the retina. A concave (diverging) lens corrects this by spreading light rays slightly before they enter the eye, moving the focal point back onto the retina.

questions.question: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to:-

options.text: change the curvature of the lens in order to focus on objects at different distances
change the size of the pupil to allow more or less light into the eye

questions.explanation: Accommodation is the process by which the ciliary muscles change the shape (curvature) of the lens to focus on objects at different distances. For near objects, the lens becomes more convex (rounded); for distant objects, it flattens. With age, the lens loses elasticity, reducing accommodation ability (presbyopia).

questions.question: During the approach to land on an unfamiliar upward sloping runway a pilot may have a tendency to:-
questions.explanation: An upward sloping runway creates the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is (the runway appears shorter/closer). The pilot may unconsciously fly a lower approach to make the picture look 'normal'. Conversely, a downward sloping runway creates the illusion of being too low, leading to a high approach.

questions.question: During the approach to land on a very wide unfamiliar runway a pilot may have a tendency to:-
questions.explanation: A wider-than-normal runway creates the illusion that the aircraft is lower than it actually is (the runway appears closer). The pilot may fly a higher approach. Conversely, a narrower-than-normal runway creates the illusion of being too high, leading to a dangerously low approach. Always use VASIS/PAPI if available.

questions.question: The vestibular apparatus comprises the:-

options.text: semi-circular canals and the otolith organs
semi-circular canals and the Eustachian tube

questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus (balance organ) in the inner ear consists of: (1) Three semi-circular canals — detect angular (rotational) accelerations in three planes, (2) Otolith organs (utricle and saccule) — detect linear accelerations and gravity. Together they provide the brain with information about the body's orientation and movement.

questions.question: Presbycusis is the term used to define:-

options.text: a decrease in hearing ability with age
hearing loss due to noise exposure

questions.explanation: Presbycusis is the gradual, natural loss of hearing that occurs with ageing. It typically affects high-frequency sounds first. It is a sensorineural (inner ear) condition and is irreversible. Pilots should have regular hearing tests as part of their medical examinations.

questions.question: Vertigo is:-
questions.explanation: Vertigo is a false sensation of rotation — the pilot feels that they or their surroundings are spinning when no actual rotation is occurring. It is caused by conflicting signals from the vestibular system, visual system, and proprioceptive system. In flight, vertigo can be extremely dangerous and must be countered by trusting the instruments.

questions.question: Spatial disorientation is usually a temporary condition which:-

options.text: should be treated by looking at and believing the aircraft flight instruments
should be treated by closing the eyes

questions.explanation: Spatial disorientation occurs when the brain receives conflicting information from the senses about the aircraft's attitude and motion. The treatment is to trust and believe the flight instruments, not the body's sensations. The vestibular system is unreliable in flight — it evolved for ground-based movement, not aviation.

questions.question: Non-conductive, or noise-induced, hearing loss:-

options.text: is associated with the inner ear and is usually irreversible
is associated with the outer ear and is temporary

questions.explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss (sensorineural) results from damage to the hair cells in the cochlea (inner ear). It is usually permanent and irreversible. Prolonged exposure to loud noise (engine noise, headset use) causes progressive damage. Prevention: use noise-attenuating headsets, limit exposure time, and use ear protection.

questions.question: Conductive hearing loss is:-

options.text: associated with the outer or middle ear and is either temporary or can be reversed
associated with the inner ear and is always permanent

questions.explanation: Conductive hearing loss involves the outer or middle ear — sound is not conducted efficiently to the inner ear. Causes include: ear wax blockage, ear infections, perforated eardrum, or fluid in the middle ear. It is often temporary or treatable with medication or surgery, unlike sensorineural (inner ear) loss which is usually permanent.

questions.question: The term tinnitus is used to define:-

options.text: the natural loss of hearing with age

questions.explanation: Tinnitus is the perception of sound (ringing, buzzing, hissing) in the ears when no external sound is present. It can be caused by: noise exposure, ear infections, certain medications, or age-related hearing loss. Tinnitus can be distracting and may interfere with communication in the cockpit.

questions.question: A method which may be used to help passengers avoid airsickness is to:-

options.text: have them fix their eyes in the distance on the natural horizon
have them look at the instruments

questions.explanation: Motion sickness is caused by conflicting signals between the visual and vestibular systems. Fixing the eyes on the distant horizon provides a stable visual reference that matches the vestibular input, reducing the conflict. Other prevention methods: fresh air, avoiding heavy meals before flight, sitting in the front, and avoiding reading.

questions.question: The symptoms of motion sickness include:-
questions.explanation: Motion sickness symptoms progress through stages: (1) Pallor (pale skin), (2) Sweating, (3) Nausea, (4) Vomiting. Other symptoms include yawning, drowsiness, and general discomfort. The condition results from sensory conflict — the vestibular system detects motion that the eyes do not confirm, or vice versa.

questions.question: The best treatment for a pilot suffering from acute fatigue is:-

options.text: continuing to fly to build endurance

questions.explanation: Acute fatigue is short-term tiredness caused by physical or mental exertion, lack of sleep, or stress. It is effectively treated by adequate rest and natural sleep. A fatigued pilot has degraded performance: slower reactions, poor judgement, reduced attention, and increased error rate. Never fly when fatigued.

questions.question: If a passenger is observed suddenly suffering from severe chest pains and then collapses, the cause is likely to be:-
questions.explanation: Sudden severe chest pain followed by collapse is characteristic of a heart attack (myocardial infarction). The pilot should: land as soon as possible, administer first aid (loosen clothing, keep patient comfortable), call for medical assistance, and if trained, perform CPR if the patient becomes unresponsive.

questions.question: Fainting is caused by:-

options.text: a reduced flow of blood to the brain

questions.explanation: Fainting (syncope) is caused by a temporary reduction in blood flow to the brain. Causes include: low blood pressure, standing up too quickly, dehydration, heat, emotional stress, or prolonged standing. In flight, positive G-forces can reduce blood flow to the brain, causing grey-out or blackout.

questions.question: Following scuba diving, a pilot:-
questions.explanation: After scuba diving, a pilot must wait at least 24 hours before flying. During diving, nitrogen dissolves in the body tissues under increased pressure. If the pilot ascends to altitude too soon, the reduced pressure can cause nitrogen bubbles to form in the body (decompression sickness / 'the bends'), which can be incapacitating or fatal.

questions.question: If a passenger is observed suffering from mild chest pains, dizziness, breathlessness and a pale complexion the cause is likely to be:-
questions.explanation: Angina pectoris is characterised by mild to moderate chest pain, often with dizziness, breathlessness, and pallor. Unlike a heart attack, angina pain usually subsides with rest. It is caused by temporary insufficient blood supply to the heart muscle. The patient should rest, and the pilot should land as soon as practicable.

questions.question: The symptoms of low blood glucose (blood sugar) include a sensation of dizziness and shaking. This can be corrected:-
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) causes dizziness, shaking, sweating, confusion, and weakness. The brain depends on glucose for energy. Prevention: eat regular, balanced meals; avoid skipping meals before or during flight; carry snacks. Treatment: consume sugar or carbohydrates immediately.

questions.question: Chronic fatigue:-

options.text: occurs over a very long period and requires a prolonged recovery period
is cured by a single good night's sleep
is the same as acute fatigue

questions.explanation: Chronic fatigue builds up over weeks or months from sustained overwork, inadequate rest, poor diet, or ongoing stress. Unlike acute fatigue, it cannot be cured by a single sleep. It requires a prolonged period of rest, lifestyle changes, and possibly medical attention. Chronic fatigue significantly impairs judgement and decision-making.

questions.question: The type of sleep associated with physical rejuvenation is called:-
questions.explanation: Slow wave sleep (SWS), also called deep sleep, is associated with physical recovery and rejuvenation. It occurs mainly in the first half of the sleep period. During SWS, growth hormone is released, tissues are repaired, and the immune system is strengthened. REM sleep is associated with mental/brain rejuvenation.

questions.question: The type of sleep associated with brain rejuvenation is called:-
questions.explanation: REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep is associated with mental/brain rejuvenation, memory consolidation, and dreaming. It occurs mainly in the second half of the sleep period. Both SWS and REM sleep are essential — disruption of either leads to impaired performance. A full sleep cycle (SWS + REM) takes approximately 90 minutes.

questions.question: The most common symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning are:-
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning symptoms: headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion, drowsiness, and cherry-red skin colour (late sign). CO binds to haemoglobin 200-300 times more readily than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin which cannot carry oxygen. Sources in aircraft: exhaust leaks, cabin heater. Treatment: fresh air, 100% oxygen, land immediately.

questions.question: A leaking aircraft engine exhaust may pose a threat to aircrew and passengers because:-

options.text: increased amounts of carbon monoxide may enter the cabin

questions.explanation: A leaking exhaust system can allow carbon monoxide (CO) to enter the cabin, especially through the cabin heating system which often uses exhaust-heated air. CO is colourless and odourless, making it difficult to detect. If exhaust fumes are smelled, turn off the cabin heater, open air vents, and land as soon as possible.

questions.question: A method of processing information referred to as a closed loop system:-

options.text: requires feedback to the central decision maker
works independently of the central decision maker
is the same as an open loop system

questions.explanation: A closed loop system requires continuous feedback to the central decision maker (the brain). The pilot monitors the outcome of each action and makes adjustments. Example: maintaining altitude — the pilot checks the altimeter (feedback) and adjusts the controls accordingly. An open loop system operates without feedback (e.g., a well-practised motor skill).

questions.question: Memory which deals with the storage of information in word form is called:-
questions.explanation: Semantic memory is the part of long-term memory that stores factual information, concepts, words, language, and numbers. It is 'knowing' rather than 'remembering'. Episodic memory stores personal experiences and events. Procedural memory stores skills and how to do things (e.g., flying procedures).

questions.question: The short term or working memory is capable of dealing with a maximum of:-
questions.explanation: The working (short-term) memory can hold approximately 7 ± 2 items (5 to 9 items) of unrelated information for about 20-30 seconds. This capacity can be increased through 'chunking' — grouping related items together. For example, a phone number 0123456789 can be chunked as 012-345-6789 (3 chunks instead of 10 digits).

questions.question: Acute stress is considered to be:-
questions.explanation: Acute stress is a short-term response to an immediate threat or challenge. It triggers the 'fight or flight' response — increased heart rate, alertness, and adrenaline. Moderate acute stress can improve performance, but excessive stress degrades performance. Chronic stress is long-term and has cumulative negative effects on health and performance.

questions.question: The most likely causes of environmental, or physical stress in an aircraft are:-

options.text: noise and vibration combined with variations in temperature and humidity

questions.explanation: Environmental (physical) stressors in aviation include: noise (engine, propeller), vibration, temperature extremes (heat/cold), humidity variations, hypoxia (altitude), G-forces, and fatigue. These stressors accumulate and degrade performance. Proper aircraft maintenance, clothing, hydration, and rest help mitigate environmental stress.

questions.question: Chronic stress is usually a:-
questions.explanation: Chronic stress is long-term, ongoing stress that builds up over weeks, months, or years. It results from sustained pressures such as work overload, financial problems, relationship issues, or health concerns. Chronic stress has serious health consequences: weakened immune system, cardiovascular disease, depression, and impaired cognitive function.

questions.question: 'Environmental capture' is an error which is associated with:-
questions.explanation: Environmental capture is a skill-based error where a well-practised action is triggered by the wrong environmental cue. Example: a pilot intending to retract flaps after landing instead retracts the landing gear because both controls are similar and the action is automatic. Prevention: deliberate, conscious checking before executing critical actions.

questions.question: A motor programme is:-

options.text: a skill which is acquired by practice

questions.explanation: A motor programme is a learned sequence of movements stored in long-term memory that can be executed automatically without conscious thought. Examples: landing flare, engine start sequence, emergency drills. Motor programmes are developed through repetition and practice, freeing up mental capacity for other tasks.

questions.question: The term 'blood pressure' is used to:-

options.text: indicate the pressure of the blood against the walls of the main arteries

questions.explanation: Blood pressure is the force exerted by circulating blood against the walls of the arteries. It is measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg) and expressed as systolic/diastolic (e.g., 120/80). High blood pressure (hypertension) increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney disease. Pilots must maintain healthy blood pressure for medical certification.

questions.question: Platelets are a type of blood cell which are responsible for:-
questions.explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes) are small cell fragments in the blood that are essential for blood clotting. When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets aggregate at the site and form a plug, then trigger the clotting cascade to seal the wound. Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) causes excessive bleeding; high count increases clot risk.

questions.question: Pilots who are suffering from blocked sinuses and continue to fly may be subject to severe pain, and even suffer ear damage, particularly during:-

options.text: a climb in a non-pressurised aircraft

questions.explanation: Blocked sinuses or Eustachian tubes prevent pressure equalisation during descent. As external pressure increases, the trapped air in the sinuses cannot escape, causing severe pain (sinus barotrauma) and potentially rupturing the eardrum. During climb, expanding air can usually escape. Never fly with a head cold, sinus infection, or blocked nose.

questions.question: When crossing time zones adjustment of the body clock:-

options.text: is easier when flying from east to west
is easier when flying from west to east
is the same in both directions

questions.explanation: Westward travel (lengthening the day) is easier to adjust to than eastward travel (shortening the day) because the body's natural circadian rhythm is slightly longer than 24 hours. Flying west aligns with this tendency. Jet lag symptoms include fatigue, insomnia, digestive problems, and reduced performance. Allow approximately one day per time zone crossed for full adjustment.

questions.question: The best method for an individual to acquire sleep 'credits' is to:-

options.text: sleep for very long periods occasionally

questions.explanation: Sleep 'credits' (reserve) are best built by maintaining a consistent, regular sleep schedule with adequate duration (7-9 hours per night). Irregular sleep patterns, even if total hours are adequate, do not provide the same restorative benefits. Sleep debt cannot be fully repaid by occasional long sleeps — consistency is key.

questions.question: Chronic insomnia is often the result of:-
questions.explanation: Chronic insomnia (persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep) is often caused by long-term stress, anxiety, depression, or medical conditions. It can also result from poor sleep hygiene, shift work, or substance use. Chronic insomnia severely impairs cognitive function, mood, and health. Professional medical help should be sought.

questions.question: The tiny air sacs in the lungs which allow oxygen to diffuse into the blood and carbon dioxide to diffuse into the lungs are called:-
questions.explanation: Alveoli are microscopic air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs. Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the surrounding capillaries (blood vessels), while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled. The lungs contain approximately 300 million alveoli, providing a huge surface area for gas exchange.

questions.question: Adaptation of the eye for night vision may take up to:-
questions.explanation: Full dark adaptation (maximum sensitivity to low light) takes approximately 30 minutes. The cones adapt in about 7 minutes, but the rods require 20-30 minutes. Exposure to bright light (even briefly) destroys dark adaptation. To preserve night vision: use red cockpit lighting, avoid looking at bright lights, and allow adequate time for adaptation before night flight.

questions.question: It may be impossible to see a distant, faintly lit object at night by looking directly at it because:-

options.text: the light rays will be focused on the fovea which contains a concentration of cones
the light rays will be focused on the fovea which contains a concentration of rods

questions.explanation: The fovea (centre of the retina) contains mainly cones, which require bright light to function. At night, cones are ineffective, creating a 'blind spot' in the centre of vision. Rods (which detect dim light) are concentrated in the peripheral retina. Therefore, looking slightly to the side of a faint object (off-centre viewing) places the image on the rods, making it visible.

questions.question: Angina is characterised by:-

options.text: mild chest pains which subside on resting

questions.explanation: Angina pectoris is characterised by mild to moderate chest pain (often described as pressure, tightness, or squeezing) that is triggered by exertion or stress and relieved by rest. It is caused by temporary insufficient blood supply to the heart muscle. Unlike a heart attack, angina does not cause permanent heart damage, but it is a warning sign of heart disease.

questions.question: A situation in which a pilot makes a correct decision but initiates the incorrect reaction is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: An action slip (or lapse) is a skill-based error where the pilot knows what to do (correct decision) but executes the wrong action. Example: intending to select flaps but selecting gear instead. Slips often occur during periods of distraction, stress, or fatigue. Prevention: use checklists, verbalise actions, and maintain situational awareness.

questions.question: Skill-based behaviour consists of actions that:-

options.text: operate without the constant attention of the brain
require the conscious involvement of the brain

questions.explanation: Skill-based behaviour involves highly practised, automatic actions that require minimal conscious thought (e.g., maintaining straight and level flight, routine radio calls). This frees up mental capacity for higher-level tasks. However, skill-based behaviour is prone to slips and lapses, especially during distraction or when routines are interrupted.

questions.question: Knowledge-based behaviour is associated with:-

options.text: decisions made based on knowledge stored in the long-term memory

questions.explanation: Knowledge-based behaviour is used in novel or unfamiliar situations where no rules or procedures apply. The pilot must analyse the situation, recall relevant knowledge from long-term memory, and formulate a solution. This is the slowest and most error-prone level of decision making, but it is essential for handling emergencies and unexpected situations.

questions.question: The transfer of oxygen from the lungs to the blood is a function of:-

options.text: the low levels of oxygen in the blood only

questions.explanation: Oxygen transfer from the alveoli to the blood occurs by diffusion, driven by the pressure gradient (difference in partial pressure). Oxygen moves from high pressure (in the alveoli) to low pressure (in the blood). At altitude, the reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli reduces the pressure gradient, slowing oxygen transfer and causing hypoxia.

questions.question: As the partial pressure of oxygen decreases:-

options.text: the transfer of oxygen into the blood decreases
the transfer of oxygen into the blood increases
there is no effect on oxygen transfer

questions.explanation: As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure decreases, reducing the partial pressure of oxygen. This reduces the pressure gradient between the alveoli and the blood, slowing oxygen diffusion into the blood. The result is hypoxia — insufficient oxygen in the body tissues. Supplemental oxygen or descent restores the pressure gradient.

questions.question: As the partial pressure of oxygen increases:-

options.text: the transfer of oxygen into the blood increases
the body's demand for oxygen increases
the transfer of oxygen into the blood decreases

questions.explanation: Increasing the partial pressure of oxygen (by descending to lower altitude or using supplemental oxygen) increases the pressure gradient between the alveoli and blood, enhancing oxygen diffusion into the blood. This is why supplemental oxygen is effective in treating hypoxia — it increases the oxygen partial pressure despite reduced atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: Permanent hearing loss may result from damage to the:-
questions.explanation: The cochlea is the spiral-shaped organ in the inner ear containing hair cells that convert sound vibrations into electrical signals. Damage to these hair cells (from loud noise, disease, or ageing) causes permanent sensorineural hearing loss because hair cells cannot regenerate. Damage to the eardrum or middle ear (conductive hearing loss) is often treatable.

questions.question: Decompression sickness, associated with reduced air pressure, is characterised by:-

options.text: the formation of bubbles of nitrogen in various parts of the body

questions.explanation: Decompression sickness ('the bends') occurs when dissolved nitrogen in body tissues forms bubbles due to rapid pressure reduction. This can happen after scuba diving followed by flying, or at very high altitude. Symptoms depend on where bubbles form: joints (pain/'bends'), skin (itching/'creeps'), lungs (breathing difficulty/'chokes'), or nervous system (paralysis). Treatment: 100% oxygen, descent, hyperbaric chamber.

questions.question: With regard to decompression sickness, the pain experienced by the formation of nitrogen bubbles in the body's joints is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: The 'bends' refers to joint and limb pain caused by nitrogen bubbles forming in joints, muscles, and tendons during decompression sickness. The pain can be severe and incapacitating. Other decompression sickness manifestations: 'creeps' (skin itching), 'chokes' (lung involvement with breathing difficulty), and neurological symptoms (paralysis, sensory loss).

questions.question: With regard to decompression sickness, the itching sensation created by the formation of nitrogen bubbles in the skin is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: The 'creeps' (also called 'formication') is an itching, crawling sensation on the skin caused by nitrogen bubbles forming in subcutaneous tissues. It is usually a mild form of decompression sickness but indicates that the body is experiencing decompression stress. Any symptoms of decompression sickness require immediate descent and medical attention.

questions.question: With regard to decompression sickness, the formation of nitrogen bubbles in the lungs leads to a condition known as:-
questions.explanation: The 'chokes' is a serious form of decompression sickness where nitrogen bubbles form in the pulmonary circulation (lungs). Symptoms include: chest pain, coughing, difficulty breathing, and potentially respiratory failure. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate descent, 100% oxygen, and hyperbaric chamber treatment.

questions.question: In the human ear, angular accelerations are sensed by the:-
questions.explanation: The three semi-circular canals (oriented in three perpendicular planes) detect angular (rotational) accelerations — pitch, roll, and yaw. Each canal contains fluid (endolymph) and hair cells. When the head rotates, the fluid lags behind due to inertia, deflecting the hair cells and signalling rotation to the brain.

questions.question: In the human ear, linear accelerations are sensed by the:-
questions.explanation: The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) detect linear accelerations and the direction of gravity. They contain calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths) embedded in a gel layer over hair cells. When the head accelerates linearly or tilts, the otoliths shift, bending the hair cells and signalling the movement to the brain.

questions.question: According to Boyle's Law, providing the temperature is constant:-

options.text: as the pressure of a gas increases the volume decreases
as the pressure increases the volume increases

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: at constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant. As pressure increases, volume decreases proportionally (inverse relationship). In aviation: during climb, atmospheric pressure decreases so gas in the body (sinuses, intestines, middle ear) expands. During descent, pressure increases so gas contracts. This is why ear clearing is necessary.

questions.question: During a level turn, with no external reference, a false sense that the aircraft is flying straight and level may be felt by the pilot. During the roll out a sense of turning in the opposite direction may be felt. This is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: The 'leans' is the most common spatial disorientation illusion. If a pilot enters a turn slowly (below the semi-circular canal detection threshold), the vestibular system does not sense the turn. The pilot feels straight and level while actually turning. When rolling out, the vestibular system senses the roll-out as a turn in the opposite direction. Trust the instruments.

questions.question: The 'oculogravic or somatogravic illusion' is the sensation of:-

options.text: the body rotating when in fact no rotation is occurring

questions.explanation: The somatogravic illusion occurs during rapid acceleration (e.g., take-off). The otolith organs cannot distinguish between gravity and linear acceleration. The combined force vector tilts backward, creating the illusion of a nose-up pitch attitude. The pilot may unconsciously push forward, causing a dangerously low pitch attitude. Trust the attitude indicator.

questions.question: At night a stationary light which is stared at for a few seconds may appear to move. This illusion is known as:-
questions.explanation: Autokinesis is a visual illusion where a stationary point of light (e.g., a star, distant aircraft light) appears to move when stared at in darkness with no other visual references. It is caused by small, involuntary eye movements. Prevention: avoid staring at a single light; scan the area regularly; use other references if available.

questions.question: Equalisation of the pressure between the outer ear and the middle ear is achieved through the:-
questions.explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the throat, allowing pressure equalisation between the middle ear and the external environment. During altitude changes, the Eustachian tube opens (by swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva manoeuvre) to equalise pressure. Blockage causes ear pain and potential eardrum rupture.

questions.question: The transmission of electrical signals, for conversion into sound, from the ear to the brain is achieved via the:-
questions.explanation: The auditory nerve (also called the cochlear nerve or acoustic nerve) transmits electrical signals from the hair cells in the cochlea to the brain's auditory cortex, where they are interpreted as sound. Damage to the auditory nerve causes sensorineural hearing loss, which is usually permanent.

questions.question: An increase in positive 'g' may initially result in a condition known as:-
questions.explanation: During positive G-forces (e.g., pulling out of a dive or in a steep turn), blood is forced away from the head toward the feet. Grey-out is the initial stage where peripheral vision is lost but central vision remains. If G-forces continue, it progresses to tunnel vision, then blackout (complete loss of vision), and finally G-LOC (G-induced loss of consciousness).

questions.question: 'Grey out' is a condition which may occur as a result of:-
questions.explanation: Grey-out results from positive G-forces reducing blood flow to the brain and eyes. The retina is very sensitive to reduced blood supply. Grey-out typically occurs at 3-4 G in untrained individuals. Fighter pilots use G-suits and anti-G straining manoeuvres to increase G-tolerance. In GA aircraft, avoid sustained steep turns and abrupt pull-ups.

questions.question: A sudden increase in negative 'g' may result in a condition known as:-
questions.explanation: Negative G-forces (e.g., pushing over into a dive, inverted flight) force blood toward the head. Red-out occurs when excessive blood pressure in the head causes the eyes to become bloodshot and vision takes on a reddish tinge. Negative G is very uncomfortable and can cause burst blood vessels in the eyes. Most people tolerate only -2 to -3 G.

questions.question: 'Red out' is a condition which may occur as a result of:-
questions.explanation: Red-out is caused by negative G-forces forcing blood to the head and eyes. The increased blood pressure in the retinal blood vessels causes them to engorge, giving vision a red appearance. Prolonged negative G can cause permanent eye damage. Negative G should be avoided in normal flight operations.

questions.question: 'Black out' is a condition which may occur as a result of:-
questions.explanation: Blackout is complete loss of vision (while remaining conscious) caused by sustained positive G-forces reducing blood flow to the retina. It follows grey-out and tunnel vision. If G-forces continue, G-LOC (loss of consciousness) occurs. Recovery: immediately reduce G-forces. Blackout can occur at 4-6 G in untrained individuals.

questions.question: During sustained positive 'g' acceleration:-

options.text: the blood rushes away from the head causing loss of vision, grey out, or black out
the blood rushes to the head
there is no effect on blood flow

questions.explanation: Positive G-forces (tail-to-head direction) force blood away from the brain and toward the lower body. This reduces cerebral blood flow and retinal blood supply, causing progressive symptoms: grey-out → tunnel vision → blackout → G-LOC. The heart cannot pump blood 'uphill' against high G-forces. Reducing G immediately restores blood flow.

questions.question: An increase in the level of carbon dioxide in the blood:-

options.text: will cause an increase in the breathing rate
will cause a tingling sensation in the finger tips

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is the primary regulator of breathing rate. Chemoreceptors in the brain stem detect rising CO₂ levels and trigger an increase in breathing rate to expel the excess CO₂. This is why holding your breath becomes uncomfortable — not from lack of oxygen, but from CO₂ buildup. Hyperventilation reduces CO₂ below normal levels.

questions.question: The term 'chunking' is used to define the process of:-

options.text: combining data to increase the capacity of the working or short term memory
transferring information into the long term memory

questions.explanation: Chunking is a memory technique where individual pieces of information are grouped into larger, meaningful units (chunks). This increases the effective capacity of working memory. Example: the number sequence 1-9-4-5-2-0-2-5 (8 items) can be chunked as 1945-2025 (2 items: two years). Pilots use chunking for radio frequencies, clearances, and procedures.

questions.question: The condition known as cyanosis is associated with:-
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is a bluish discolouration of the skin and mucous membranes caused by insufficient oxygen in the blood (hypoxia). It is most visible in the lips, fingernails, and earlobes. Cyanosis is a late sign of hypoxia — by the time it is visible, the person is severely hypoxic. Early recognition and treatment of hypoxia is essential.

questions.question: The ability to make a judgement based on learned skills or experience is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: Perceptual judgement is rapid, intuitive decision-making based on pattern recognition from experience. An experienced pilot can 'perceive' when something is wrong (e.g., approach is too high/low) without conscious analysis. It is fast and usually accurate but can be affected by expectation bias. Cognitive judgement involves conscious, analytical thought.

questions.question: Cognitive judgement involves decision making based on:-
questions.explanation: Cognitive judgement is deliberate, analytical decision-making involving conscious thought, reasoning, and problem-solving. It is used for complex or unfamiliar situations where perceptual judgement is insufficient. Cognitive judgement is slower but more thorough. Example: calculating whether to divert due to weather involves cognitive judgement.

questions.question: Hypoxia is caused by:-

options.text: a decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen
excessive levels of carbon dioxide in the body tissues

questions.explanation: Hypoxia is insufficient oxygen reaching the body tissues. The primary cause in aviation is decreased partial pressure of oxygen at altitude (hypoxic hypoxia). Other causes: anaemia or CO poisoning (anaemic hypoxia), poor circulation (stagnant hypoxia), or cells unable to use oxygen due to alcohol/drugs (histotoxic hypoxia).

questions.question: Hyperventilation may be caused by:-

options.text: anxiety caused by a stressful situation
too little carbon dioxide in the blood

questions.explanation: Hyperventilation (over-breathing) is usually triggered by anxiety, stress, fear, or pain. The rapid, deep breathing expels too much CO₂, causing respiratory alkalosis. Symptoms: tingling extremities, dizziness, light-headedness, muscle spasms, confusion. It can mimic hypoxia. Treatment: consciously slow breathing, breathe into a paper bag, or talk/sing to regulate breathing.

questions.question: Visual acuity is:-

options.text: the ability of the eye to see clearly and distinguish fine detail
the ability to see in the dark

questions.explanation: Visual acuity is the sharpness or clarity of vision — the ability to distinguish fine detail. It is measured using eye charts (e.g., 20/20 vision). Visual acuity is best in the fovea (central vision) in bright light using cone cells. It decreases with: dim light, fatigue, hypoxia, alcohol, certain medications, and ageing. Pilots must meet minimum visual acuity standards.

questions.question: The early symptoms of hypoxia include:-

options.text: euphoria, impaired judgement, and decreased performance

questions.explanation: Early hypoxia symptoms are insidious and often unrecognised by the sufferer: euphoria (false sense of well-being), impaired judgement, decreased performance, slowed reactions, difficulty concentrating, poor coordination, and personality changes. Later symptoms: cyanosis (blue lips/nails), headache, dizziness, breathlessness, and eventually unconsciousness. The danger is that hypoxia impairs the ability to recognise hypoxia.

questions.question: The IMSAFE checklist is used to assess:-
questions.explanation: IMSAFE is a personal fitness checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating/Emotion. Pilots should use this before every flight to assess whether they are fit to fly. Any 'no' answer should prompt serious consideration of postponing the flight. Self-assessment is critical — regulations set minimums, but pilots must honestly evaluate their own condition.

questions.question: According to aviation regulations, a pilot may not fly within:-
questions.explanation: The '8 hours bottle to throttle' rule is the legal minimum, but many pilots use '12 hours bottle to throttle' or longer. Alcohol impairs judgement, coordination, vision, and reaction time. It also increases susceptibility to hypoxia. The pilot must have zero blood alcohol content when flying. Hangovers also impair performance — if you're not fit, don't fly.

questions.question: The effects of alcohol on the body:-

options.text: are magnified at altitude due to reduced oxygen availability

questions.explanation: Alcohol's effects are significantly magnified at altitude. Alcohol impairs the brain's ability to use oxygen (histotoxic hypoxia). Combined with reduced oxygen availability at altitude (hypoxic hypoxia), the effects are compounded. Even small amounts of alcohol can severely impair performance at altitude. The effective altitude is increased by approximately 2000 ft per drink.

questions.question: Over-the-counter medications:-

options.text: may have side effects that impair flying ability and should be checked before flying

questions.explanation: Many over-the-counter medications cause drowsiness, dizziness, or impaired judgement. Common culprits: antihistamines (allergy/cold medicines), sleep aids, motion sickness medications, and pain relievers. The underlying condition may also be disqualifying (e.g., a cold blocks sinuses). Rule: if you need medication, you probably shouldn't fly. Consult an aviation medical examiner if uncertain.

questions.question: Crew Resource Management (CRM) is:-

options.text: the effective use of all available resources (people, equipment, information) to achieve safe flight operations
a method of scheduling crew duty times

questions.explanation: CRM focuses on interpersonal communication, leadership, and decision-making in the cockpit. Key elements: communication, situational awareness, problem-solving, decision-making, and teamwork. CRM recognises that most accidents result from human factors, not technical failures. Even single-pilot operations benefit from CRM principles (using ATC, passengers, and other resources).

questions.question: Threat and Error Management (TEM) involves:-

options.text: identifying threats, avoiding errors, and managing consequences to maintain safety margins

questions.explanation: TEM is a framework for managing threats (external factors like weather, terrain), errors (pilot mistakes), and undesired aircraft states (deviations from intended flight path). The goal is to detect and manage threats before they lead to errors, and manage errors before they lead to undesired states. TEM promotes a proactive, non-punitive safety culture.

questions.question: The 'Swiss Cheese Model' of accident causation suggests that:-

options.text: accidents occur when holes in multiple defensive layers align, allowing a hazard to pass through
accidents are caused by a single catastrophic failure
accidents only happen to inexperienced pilots

questions.explanation: James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model shows that organisations have multiple defensive layers (training, procedures, equipment, regulations). Each layer has weaknesses ('holes'). An accident occurs when holes in all layers align, allowing a hazard to pass through. This explains why accidents typically involve multiple contributing factors, not a single cause. Prevention: strengthen all layers.

questions.question: The 'dirty dozen' in human factors refers to:-

options.text: twelve common human error precursors in aviation maintenance and operations

questions.explanation: The Dirty Dozen are twelve human factors that contribute to errors: Lack of communication, Complacency, Lack of knowledge, Distraction, Lack of teamwork, Fatigue, Lack of resources, Pressure, Lack of assertiveness, Stress, Lack of awareness, Norms (peer pressure). Originally developed for maintenance, they apply equally to flight operations. Awareness of these factors helps prevent errors.

questions.question: Confirmation bias is:-

options.text: the tendency to search for or interpret information in a way that confirms pre-existing beliefs

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias causes pilots to notice information that supports their expectations while ignoring contradictory information. Example: expecting good weather, a pilot may dismiss deteriorating conditions. Or expecting a certain runway, they may misread the identifier. Prevention: actively seek disconfirming evidence, use checklists, and maintain an open, questioning mindset.

questions.question: The 'get-home-itis' or 'plan continuation bias' refers to:-

options.text: the tendency to continue with the original plan despite changing circumstances that suggest an alternative course of action

questions.explanation: Get-home-itis (plan continuation bias) is a dangerous tendency to press on toward the destination despite deteriorating weather, fuel concerns, or other hazards. Psychological factors: commitment to the plan, pressure to arrive, reluctance to 'waste' time/money, and optimism bias. Prevention: set personal minimums, have alternate plans, and be willing to divert or turn back.

questions.question: Situational awareness is:-

options.text: the accurate perception and understanding of all factors affecting the flight

questions.explanation: Situational awareness (SA) is knowing what is happening around you and understanding how information, events, and actions will affect goals and objectives. Three levels: (1) Perception of elements, (2) Comprehension of their meaning, (3) Projection of future status. Loss of SA is a major accident contributor. Maintain SA through scanning, communication, and anticipation.

questions.question: The 'sterile cockpit' rule means:-

options.text: no non-essential activities or conversations during critical phases of flight
the cockpit must be physically clean

questions.explanation: The sterile cockpit rule (below 10,000 ft for commercial operations, or during critical phases for all flights) prohibits non-essential activities and conversations. Critical phases: taxi, take-off, landing, and any operations below 10,000 ft. The rule reduces distractions during high-workload periods. Essential communication (checklists, ATC, safety-related) is permitted and encouraged.

questions.question: Fixation (also called 'tunnel vision' in decision-making) is:-

options.text: focusing attention on one issue to the exclusion of other important factors

questions.explanation: Fixation occurs when a pilot becomes so focused on one problem (e.g., a malfunctioning instrument, a navigation issue) that they neglect other critical tasks like flying the aircraft. This can lead to controlled flight into terrain or loss of control. Prevention: maintain the priority — aviate, navigate, communicate. Delegate tasks if possible.

questions.question: The DECIDE model for decision-making stands for:-

options.text: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
Determine, Execute, Calculate, Initiate, Decide, End
Delay, Estimate, Continue, Ignore, Decide, Exit
Detect, Eliminate, Continue, Identify, Delay, Execute

questions.explanation: DECIDE is a structured decision-making process: Detect the problem, Estimate the need to react, Choose a desirable outcome, Identify actions, Do the necessary action, Evaluate the effect. This systematic approach helps prevent hasty decisions and ensures all factors are considered. It is particularly useful for non-time-critical decisions.

questions.question: Dehydration during flight can cause:-

options.text: fatigue, headaches, dizziness, and impaired decision-making

questions.explanation: Dehydration is common in flight due to low humidity in the cabin, breathing dry air, and inadequate fluid intake. Even mild dehydration (2% body weight loss) impairs cognitive function, reaction time, and physical performance. Symptoms: thirst, fatigue, headache, dizziness, dark urine. Prevention: drink water regularly before and during flight; avoid caffeine and alcohol which are diuretics.

questions.question: Caffeine consumption:-

options.text: can temporarily improve alertness but may cause dehydration and sleep disruption

questions.explanation: Caffeine is a stimulant that can temporarily improve alertness and concentration. However, it is a diuretic (increases urination, contributing to dehydration), can cause jitteriness and anxiety in high doses, and disrupts sleep quality if consumed late in the day. Caffeine does not cure fatigue — only sleep does. Use caffeine judiciously and maintain hydration.

questions.question: The circadian rhythm is:-

options.text: the body's internal 24-hour biological clock that regulates sleep-wake cycles

questions.explanation: The circadian rhythm is the body's internal clock that regulates sleep-wake cycles, hormone release, body temperature, and other physiological processes on a roughly 24-hour cycle. It is influenced by light exposure. Disruption (shift work, time zone changes, irregular schedules) causes fatigue, impaired performance, and health problems. Maintain regular sleep schedules when possible.

questions.question: The 'window of circadian low' (WOCL) is:-

options.text: the period between 0200-0600 when the body is least alert and performance is poorest

questions.explanation: The WOCL (typically 0200-0600 local time) is when the circadian rhythm causes the lowest alertness and poorest performance. Body temperature is lowest, reaction times are slowest, and errors are most likely. There is a secondary dip in the early afternoon (1400-1600). Avoid critical tasks during WOCL if possible; use extra vigilance if flying during these hours.

questions.question: Microsleeps are:-

options.text: brief episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds that occur involuntarily when severely fatigued

questions.explanation: Microsleeps are involuntary sleep episodes lasting 1-30 seconds that occur when the brain is severely sleep-deprived. During a microsleep, the person may appear awake but is functionally asleep — eyes may be open but they are not processing information. In flight, even a 5-second microsleep can be catastrophic. If experiencing microsleeps, land immediately.

questions.question: A strategic nap (planned short sleep) before a long flight:-

options.text: can improve alertness and performance if timed correctly (20-30 minutes)

questions.explanation: A strategic nap of 20-30 minutes can improve alertness without causing sleep inertia (grogginess upon waking). Naps longer than 30 minutes risk entering deep sleep, causing sleep inertia that can last 15-30 minutes. A pre-flight nap can be beneficial if the pilot is already well-rested. Naps cannot substitute for adequate nighttime sleep.

questions.question: The hazardous attitude of 'anti-authority' is characterised by:-

options.text: the belief that rules and regulations don't apply to me

questions.explanation: The five hazardous attitudes are: Anti-authority ('Don't tell me'), Impulsivity ('Do it quickly'), Invulnerability ('It won't happen to me'), Macho ('I can do it'), Resignation ('What's the use?'). Each has an antidote: Anti-authority → 'Follow the rules, they're usually right'. Recognising and countering hazardous attitudes is essential for safe decision-making.

questions.question: The hazardous attitude of 'invulnerability' is characterised by:-

options.text: the belief that accidents happen to other people, not to me

questions.explanation: Invulnerability ('It won't happen to me') is the false belief that one is immune to accidents. This leads to risk-taking and complacency. Antidote: 'It could happen to me'. Statistics show that most accident pilots were experienced and confident — overconfidence is dangerous. Maintain a healthy respect for risks and always use proper procedures.

questions.question: The hazardous attitude of 'macho' is characterised by:-

options.text: the need to prove oneself by taking unnecessary risks

questions.explanation: Macho ('I can do it') involves taking risks to prove one's ability or toughness. Examples: flying in marginal weather to show skill, refusing to divert despite fuel concerns, or attempting a landing beyond one's capability. Antidote: 'Taking chances is foolish'. True professionalism means knowing your limitations and making conservative decisions.

questions.question: The hazardous attitude of 'resignation' is characterised by:-

options.text: the belief that events are beyond one's control and there's nothing one can do

questions.explanation: Resignation ('What's the use?') is a passive attitude where the pilot feels helpless to affect outcomes. This leads to failure to take corrective action when problems arise. Antidote: 'I'm not helpless, I can make a difference'. Pilots must believe they can control the situation and take appropriate action. Learned helplessness is dangerous in aviation.

questions.question: The hazardous attitude of 'impulsivity' is characterised by:-

options.text: the need to do something immediately without thinking it through

questions.explanation: Impulsivity ('Do it quickly') is the tendency to act without thinking, to react immediately without considering alternatives or consequences. Examples: making a hasty decision to continue VFR into IMC, or rushing a landing without proper preparation. Antidote: 'Not so fast, think first'. Take time to assess the situation and consider options before acting.

questions.question: Rule-based behaviour involves:-

options.text: following established procedures and rules to handle familiar situations
creating new solutions for every situation

questions.explanation: Rule-based behaviour is the intermediate level of performance where pilots apply learned rules and procedures to familiar situations. Example: following the engine failure checklist. It requires conscious thought but less than knowledge-based behaviour. Errors occur when the wrong rule is applied or when rules are incomplete. Proper training and SOPs reduce rule-based errors.

questions.question: An error chain in aviation refers to:-

options.text: a sequence of events or errors that, when combined, lead to an accident

questions.explanation: Most accidents result from a chain of events (error chain) rather than a single cause. Each link is a contributing factor: poor planning, weather deterioration, fatigue, pressure to complete the flight, poor decision-making. Breaking any link in the chain prevents the accident. This is why pilots must recognize developing situations and take corrective action early.

questions.question: Normalization of deviance refers to:-

options.text: the gradual acceptance of non-standard practices as normal when nothing bad happens

questions.explanation: Normalization of deviance occurs when repeated violations or shortcuts without immediate negative consequences lead to acceptance of the deviant behaviour as normal. Example: consistently flying with less fuel reserve than required. Eventually, the deviance becomes the norm, increasing risk. Prevention: maintain strict adherence to standards and procedures regardless of past 'success'.

questions.question: The 'startle effect' in aviation refers to:-

options.text: the temporary cognitive impairment caused by an unexpected event

questions.explanation: The startle effect is an involuntary physiological and psychological response to sudden, unexpected events. It causes temporary cognitive impairment: delayed reactions, fixation, tunnel vision, and inappropriate responses. Training and preparation help reduce startle effects. Simulator training exposing pilots to unexpected events improves their ability to manage startle and respond appropriately.

questions.question: Complacency in aviation is:-

options.text: a state of self-satisfaction accompanied by reduced vigilance and attention

questions.explanation: Complacency develops from routine, familiarity, and overconfidence. The pilot becomes less vigilant, skips checks, and assumes everything is normal. Complacency is dangerous because it reduces the pilot's ability to detect and respond to developing problems. Prevention: maintain discipline, use checklists, and actively look for potential problems even on routine flights.

questions.question: The 'authority gradient' in a cockpit refers to:-

options.text: the balance of decision-making power between crew members

questions.explanation: Authority gradient is the perceived or actual difference in power/authority between crew members. A steep gradient (captain dominates) can prevent junior crew from speaking up about safety concerns. A flat gradient (excessive equality) can lead to confusion about who is in command. The optimal gradient allows open communication while maintaining clear command authority. CRM training addresses this.

questions.question: Assertiveness in aviation means:-

options.text: clearly and respectfully stating concerns or disagreements when safety is at risk

questions.explanation: Assertiveness is the ability to clearly express concerns, opinions, or disagreements in a respectful, professional manner. It is essential for safety — crew members must speak up when they see potential problems. Lack of assertiveness has contributed to many accidents where crew members noticed problems but failed to speak up. CRM training emphasizes assertiveness techniques.

questions.question: The 'recency effect' in memory means:-

options.text: items learned or experienced most recently are remembered best

questions.explanation: The recency effect means recent information is more easily recalled than older information. In aviation, this affects training retention — skills not practiced recently deteriorate. This is why recurrent training and currency requirements exist. Pilots should practice emergency procedures regularly to maintain proficiency, not just during initial training or flight reviews.

questions.question: The 'primacy effect' in learning means:-

options.text: first impressions and initial learning are remembered best and are hardest to change

questions.explanation: The primacy effect means information learned first is retained best and is most resistant to change. In flight training, this emphasizes the importance of correct initial instruction — bad habits learned early are very difficult to unlearn. Instructors must ensure students learn correct techniques from the start. First impressions of procedures, aircraft handling, etc., are lasting.

questions.question: Prospective memory is:-

options.text: remembering to perform an intended action in the future

questions.explanation: Prospective memory is remembering to do something at a future time (e.g., remember to switch fuel tanks in 30 minutes, remember to contact ATC at a certain point). It is vulnerable to interruption and distraction. Aids: timers, written notes, checklists, and verbal reminders. Prospective memory failures can have serious consequences in aviation.

questions.question: The 'availability heuristic' is:-

options.text: judging the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic causes people to overestimate the probability of events that are easily recalled (recent, dramatic, or personally experienced). Example: after hearing about a recent accident, a pilot may overestimate the risk of that type of accident. This can lead to either excessive caution or, conversely, dismissing risks that haven't been recently publicized. Maintain objective risk assessment.

questions.question: Optimism bias is:-

options.text: the tendency to believe that bad things are less likely to happen to oneself than to others

questions.explanation: Optimism bias causes pilots to underestimate risks and overestimate their ability to handle situations. Examples: 'The weather will improve', 'I can make it on this fuel', 'That won't happen to me'. While some optimism is healthy, excessive optimism leads to poor risk management. Balance optimism with realistic assessment of risks and honest evaluation of capabilities.

questions.question: The 'sunk cost fallacy' in decision-making is:-

options.text: continuing a course of action because of past investment (time, money, effort) rather than current circumstances
making decisions based only on current information

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy causes pilots to continue a flight because they've already invested time, money, or effort, even when current conditions suggest diverting or turning back. Example: 'We've come this far, we might as well continue' despite deteriorating weather. Sunk costs are irrelevant to current decisions — base decisions on current and future factors, not past investment.

questions.question: The 'bystander effect' in aviation can lead to:-

options.text: individuals failing to take action because they assume someone else will
immediate action by all crew members

questions.explanation: The bystander effect occurs when multiple people witness a problem but each assumes someone else will act. In multi-crew operations, this can lead to critical tasks being missed because each crew member thinks the other is handling it. Prevention: clear task assignment, explicit communication, and closed-loop communication (acknowledge receipt and understanding of instructions).

questions.question: Closed-loop communication involves:-

options.text: the receiver repeating back the message to confirm understanding

questions.explanation: Closed-loop communication ensures messages are correctly received and understood: (1) Sender transmits message, (2) Receiver acknowledges and reads back, (3) Sender confirms or corrects. This is standard in ATC communications and should be used in cockpit communications for critical items. It prevents misunderstandings and ensures all parties have the same information.

questions.question: The 'just culture' concept in aviation safety means:-

options.text: a culture that distinguishes between honest mistakes and reckless behaviour, encouraging reporting without fear of punishment for honest errors

questions.explanation: Just culture recognizes that humans make errors and that most errors result from system weaknesses, not individual incompetence. It encourages reporting and learning from errors without fear of punishment, while still holding individuals accountable for reckless behaviour or willful violations. This approach improves safety by identifying and fixing system problems rather than just blaming individuals.

questions.question: Hindsight bias is:-

options.text: the tendency to see past events as having been predictable after they have occurred
inability to learn from the past

questions.explanation: Hindsight bias ('I knew it all along') makes past events seem more predictable than they actually were. In accident investigation, this can lead to unfair blame: 'The pilot should have known'. In reality, the pilot had incomplete information and time pressure. Hindsight bias can prevent learning the real lessons from accidents. Investigators must reconstruct the situation as it appeared to the pilot at the time.

questions.question: The 'fight or flight' response is:-

options.text: an automatic physiological response to perceived threat, preparing the body for action

questions.explanation: The fight-or-flight response is triggered by the sympathetic nervous system in response to perceived threats. Physical changes: increased heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, muscle tension, and adrenaline release. While useful for physical threats, it can impair fine motor skills and complex decision-making needed in aviation emergencies. Training helps manage this response.

questions.question: The Yerkes-Dodson Law states that:-

options.text: performance improves with arousal/stress up to an optimal point, then declines with further stress
performance always declines with any stress

questions.explanation: The Yerkes-Dodson Law describes an inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance. Too little arousal (boredom, complacency) leads to poor performance. Moderate arousal (alertness, focus) produces optimal performance. Excessive arousal (high stress, panic) degrades performance. The optimal level varies with task complexity — simple tasks tolerate higher arousal; complex tasks require lower arousal.

questions.question: Stress management techniques for pilots include:-

options.text: regular exercise, adequate sleep, time management, and relaxation techniques

questions.explanation: Effective stress management: regular physical exercise, adequate sleep (7-9 hours), healthy diet, time management, relaxation techniques (deep breathing, meditation), social support, and work-life balance. Avoid unhealthy coping mechanisms: alcohol, drugs, excessive caffeine, or denial. Chronic stress requires professional help. Managing stress improves health, performance, and safety.

questions.question: The 'Coriolis illusion' in spatial disorientation occurs when:-

options.text: the pilot makes a head movement during a prolonged turn, causing a false sensation of rotation in a different plane
the aircraft is in straight and level flight

questions.explanation: The Coriolis illusion occurs when a pilot makes a head movement (looking down at a chart, turning to check something) during a prolonged constant-rate turn. The head movement stimulates a different semi-circular canal, creating a false sensation of rotation in another plane (e.g., tumbling). This is extremely disorienting. Prevention: avoid head movements during turns in IMC; if necessary, move slowly.

questions.question: The 'graveyard spiral' is:-

options.text: a descending turn that the pilot does not recognize, often leading to a fatal crash

questions.explanation: The graveyard spiral results from 'the leans'. In IMC, the pilot inadvertently enters a gentle turn. After the semi-circular canals adapt, the pilot feels straight and level while actually turning and descending. Noticing the descent, the pilot pulls back, tightening the spiral. The solution: trust the instruments, level the wings first, then gently recover from the descent.

questions.question: The 'black hole approach' illusion occurs when:-

options.text: approaching a runway at night over dark terrain or water with no visual references, creating the illusion of being too high

questions.explanation: The black hole illusion occurs on night approaches over dark, featureless terrain or water with no visible horizon or ground lights — only the runway lights are visible. This creates the illusion of being higher than actual, leading to a dangerously low approach. Prevention: use VASI/PAPI, maintain proper approach speed and descent rate, cross-check altimeter, and be aware of the illusion.

questions.question: The 'empty field myopia' phenomenon is:-

options.text: the eyes focusing at a near point (1-2 metres) when there are no distant objects to focus on, reducing ability to see distant traffic

questions.explanation: Empty field myopia occurs when flying in conditions with no visual references (haze, uniform cloud, darkness). The eyes automatically focus at a resting point of 1-2 metres rather than infinity, making distant objects (other aircraft) appear blurred and difficult to detect. Prevention: actively focus on distant points, scan systematically, and blink regularly to maintain focus.

questions.question: The most effective scanning technique for detecting other aircraft is:-

options.text: a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements with brief fixations

questions.explanation: Effective visual scanning uses a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements (10-15° segments) with 1-2 second fixations in each segment. This allows the eyes to focus and the brain to process information. Continuous sweeping or staring reduces detection ability. Scan the entire visual field systematically, including above, below, and behind (using mirrors or turning).

questions.question: The 'see and avoid' principle for collision avoidance:-

options.text: is the pilot's primary responsibility but has limitations, especially in poor visibility or high-speed closure

questions.explanation: See-and-avoid is fundamental to collision avoidance but has significant limitations: limited human visual capabilities, blind spots, closure rates, distractions, and environmental factors (haze, sun glare). Pilots must use all available resources: ATC traffic information, TCAS/TAS, position lights, and proper lookout. Maintain vigilance and use systematic scanning.

questions.question: White blood cells (leukocytes) are responsible for:-
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leukocytes) are part of the immune system and defend the body against infection and disease. There are several types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Abnormal white cell counts can indicate infection, immune disorders, or other health problems that may affect fitness to fly.
