questions.question: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin which:-

options.text: binds to oxygen in the lungs and transports it to body tissues

questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen in the lungs (forming oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it in the tissues. Each haemoglobin molecule can carry four oxygen molecules. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin 200-300 times more readily than oxygen, which is why CO poisoning is so dangerous.

questions.question: Normal oxygen saturation (SpO₂) in healthy individuals at sea level is:-
questions.explanation: Normal oxygen saturation is 95-100% at sea level. This represents the percentage of haemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen. SpO₂ below 90% indicates hypoxia. At altitude, SpO₂ decreases: at 10,000 ft, typical SpO₂ is 85-90%; at 15,000 ft, 70-85%. Pulse oximeters measure SpO₂ and can detect hypoxia before symptoms appear.

questions.question: A pulse oximeter measures:-

options.text: oxygen saturation in the blood and heart rate

questions.explanation: A pulse oximeter is a non-invasive device that measures oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and heart rate. It works by shining light through a fingertip or earlobe and measuring absorption. Pilots can use pulse oximeters to monitor for hypoxia during high-altitude flights. However, they have limitations: inaccurate in carbon monoxide poisoning (CO-haemoglobin reads as oxyhaemoglobin).

questions.question: The primary symptom that distinguishes hyperventilation from hypoxia is:-

options.text: tingling in the extremities (fingers, toes, lips)

questions.explanation: Tingling (paraesthesia) in the fingers, toes, and around the mouth is characteristic of hyperventilation, caused by low CO₂ levels affecting nerve function. Both hypoxia and hyperventilation cause dizziness and light-headedness, making them difficult to distinguish. If uncertain, treat for hypoxia first (descend, use oxygen), then address hyperventilation if symptoms persist.

questions.question: The Valsalva manoeuvre is used to:-

options.text: equalize pressure in the middle ear by forcing air through the Eustachian tubes

questions.explanation: The Valsalva manoeuvre (pinching the nose and gently blowing) forces air through the Eustachian tubes to equalize middle ear pressure during descent. Use it gently to avoid damaging the eardrum. Alternative methods: swallowing, yawning, or chewing gum. Never perform Valsalva during ascent (pressure equalizes naturally) or if you have a cold (can force infection into the middle ear).

questions.question: Barotrauma refers to:-

options.text: injury caused by pressure changes affecting gas-filled body cavities

questions.explanation: Barotrauma is tissue damage caused by pressure changes in gas-filled spaces: middle ear, sinuses, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and teeth (with cavities or recent dental work). Most common in aviation: ear and sinus barotrauma during descent when pressure cannot equalize. Prevention: avoid flying with congestion; equalize pressure frequently during descent.

questions.question: Flicker vertigo can be caused by:-

options.text: sunlight flickering through a rotating propeller at certain frequencies

questions.explanation: Flicker vertigo is a rare condition caused by flickering light at frequencies of 4-20 Hz (cycles per second), such as sunlight through a propeller. It can cause disorientation, nausea, seizures (in susceptible individuals), or unconsciousness. Prevention: change heading slightly, adjust sun visor, wear sunglasses, or alter RPM if possible. If symptoms occur, look away from the flicker source.

questions.question: The 'big sky theory' in collision avoidance is:-

options.text: a false sense of security based on the belief that the sky is so large that collisions are unlikely

questions.explanation: The 'big sky theory' is a dangerous misconception that collisions are unlikely because the sky is vast. In reality, aircraft converge at certain points (airports, navigation fixes, airways), and closure rates can be very high. Mid-air collisions do occur. Never rely on the big sky theory — maintain vigilant lookout, use ATC services, and follow proper procedures.

questions.question: The greatest collision risk exists when another aircraft:-

options.text: appears stationary in your field of view (constant bearing, decreasing range)
is moving rapidly across your field of view

questions.explanation: If another aircraft maintains a constant bearing (appears stationary in your windscreen) and the distance is decreasing, you are on a collision course. Aircraft on collision courses show no apparent motion — they just get bigger. Aircraft that appear to move across your field of view will pass clear. Always investigate any aircraft that appears stationary.

questions.question: Presbyopia is:-

options.text: age-related loss of the eye's ability to focus on near objects

questions.explanation: Presbyopia is the gradual loss of the eye's ability to focus on close objects, occurring with age (typically after 40). It is caused by hardening of the lens, reducing accommodation. Pilots with presbyopia need reading glasses or bifocals for charts and instruments. This is normal ageing and does not disqualify pilots, but corrective lenses must be worn when required.

questions.question: Astigmatism is:-

options.text: irregular curvature of the cornea or lens causing blurred or distorted vision

questions.explanation: Astigmatism is caused by irregular curvature of the cornea or lens, causing light to focus at multiple points rather than a single point on the retina. This results in blurred or distorted vision at all distances. It is corrected with cylindrical lenses (glasses or contact lenses). Uncorrected astigmatism can cause eyestrain, headaches, and reduced visual acuity.

questions.question: Colour vision deficiency (colour blindness) most commonly affects:-

options.text: the ability to distinguish red and green
the ability to see all colours

questions.explanation: The most common form of colour blindness is red-green colour deficiency, affecting about 8% of males and 0.5% of females. It is usually inherited and involves defective cone cells. In aviation, colour vision is important for interpreting lights (navigation, position, warning lights) and charts. Pilots with colour deficiency may have restrictions or require special testing.

questions.question: The blind spot in the eye is caused by:-

options.text: the optic nerve exit point where there are no photoreceptors

questions.explanation: The blind spot (optic disc) is the point where the optic nerve exits the retina. There are no photoreceptors (rods or cones) at this location, creating a small blind area in each eye's visual field. Normally, the brain fills in this gap using information from the other eye and surrounding areas. The blind spot is about 15° temporal to the fovea.

questions.question: Sunglasses for flying should:-

options.text: be non-polarized and provide UV protection without being too dark

questions.explanation: Aviation sunglasses should: (1) Provide UV protection, (2) Be non-polarized (polarized lenses can make LCD displays invisible and create false reflections on the windscreen), (3) Not be too dark (impairs ability to see instruments and detect other aircraft), (4) Be neutral grey or green tint (preserves colour recognition). Remove sunglasses when entering cloud or at night.

questions.question: The 'cocktail party effect' in selective attention means:-

options.text: the ability to focus on one conversation while filtering out background noise
inability to hear anything in noise

questions.explanation: The cocktail party effect is the brain's ability to selectively attend to one auditory source while filtering out others. In aviation, this allows pilots to focus on ATC communications while filtering out other radio traffic. However, important information can be missed if attention is too narrowly focused. Maintain awareness of the overall radio environment.

questions.question: Inattentional blindness is:-

options.text: failing to see something in plain sight because attention is focused elsewhere

questions.explanation: Inattentional blindness (also called 'looked but failed to see') occurs when a person fails to notice something in their visual field because their attention is focused on something else. In aviation, this can cause pilots to miss other aircraft, obstacles, or instrument indications. Prevention: systematic scanning, cross-checking, and avoiding fixation on single tasks.

questions.question: Change blindness is:-

options.text: failing to detect changes in the visual environment when attention is diverted

questions.explanation: Change blindness is the failure to detect changes in the visual scene when attention is briefly interrupted or diverted. Example: failing to notice an altimeter change during a momentary distraction. This demonstrates that we don't see everything in our visual field — only what we attend to. Prevention: systematic instrument scanning and cross-checking.

questions.question: The 'useful field of view' refers to:-

options.text: the area from which information can be extracted in a single glance without eye movement

questions.explanation: The useful field of view is the area where information can be processed in a single fixation (typically 10-15° around the fixation point). It is much smaller than the total visual field (about 200°). This is why systematic scanning with multiple fixations is necessary — you cannot process the entire visual field at once. Stress and workload further reduce the useful field of view.

questions.question: Expectation bias in perception means:-

options.text: seeing what you expect to see rather than what is actually there

questions.explanation: Expectation bias causes people to perceive what they expect rather than what is actually present. Examples: reading an altimeter as 3,500 ft when it actually shows 2,500 ft because you expect to be at 3,500 ft; or misidentifying a runway because you expect a different runway. Prevention: cross-check, verify, and question your perceptions.

questions.question: The 'startle reflex' differs from the 'startle effect' in that the reflex is:-

options.text: an immediate, involuntary physical reaction (flinch, gasp) lasting less than a second

questions.explanation: The startle reflex is an immediate, involuntary physical reaction (muscle contraction, flinch, gasp) to a sudden stimulus, lasting less than one second. The startle effect is the subsequent cognitive and performance impairment that can last several seconds or longer. Both can affect pilot performance. Training and mental preparation help manage both the reflex and the effect.

questions.question: Task saturation occurs when:-

options.text: the pilot's workload exceeds their capacity to process information and perform tasks
the pilot has too little to do
the aircraft is full of passengers

questions.explanation: Task saturation occurs when workload exceeds the pilot's capacity to manage all required tasks. This leads to: delayed responses, errors, fixation, and task shedding (dropping important tasks). Prevention: prioritize (aviate, navigate, communicate), delegate when possible, simplify (reduce unnecessary tasks), and maintain proficiency to increase capacity. Recognize early signs and reduce workload.

questions.question: The 'aviate, navigate, communicate' priority hierarchy means:-

options.text: first maintain aircraft control, then navigate, then communicate — in that order of priority
communicate first, then navigate, then aviate

questions.explanation: Aviate, navigate, communicate is the fundamental priority hierarchy: (1) Aviate — maintain aircraft control and fly the aircraft safely, (2) Navigate — know where you are and where you're going, (3) Communicate — talk to ATC and others. In an emergency, never sacrifice aircraft control to navigate or communicate. Fly the aircraft first, always.

questions.question: Personal minimums are:-

options.text: self-imposed limits more conservative than regulatory minimums, based on experience and proficiency

questions.explanation: Personal minimums are self-imposed operational limits (weather, crosswind, fuel reserves, etc.) that are more conservative than regulatory minimums. They account for individual experience, proficiency, aircraft capability, and conditions. Example: a pilot might set personal minimums of 3 miles visibility and 1500 ft ceiling, even though VFR minimums are 3 miles and 1000 ft. Adjust personal minimums as experience grows.

questions.question: The PAVE checklist for risk assessment evaluates:-
questions.explanation: PAVE is a risk assessment tool: Pilot (experience, currency, fitness), Aircraft (performance, equipment, airworthiness), enVironment (weather, terrain, airports), External pressures (schedule, passengers, financial). Evaluate each category and identify risk factors. High risk in multiple categories suggests postponing or canceling the flight.

questions.question: The 5P model for continuous risk management includes:-
questions.explanation: The 5P model is used at key decision points during flight: Plan (route, weather, fuel), Plane (aircraft status, equipment), Pilot (fitness, proficiency), Passengers (needs, distractions), Programming (automation, navigation setup). Review the 5Ps at: preflight, pre-takeoff, hourly or at waypoints, pre-descent, and when conditions change. This maintains situational awareness and identifies emerging risks.

questions.question: The 3P model for aeronautical decision-making stands for:-
questions.explanation: The 3P model is a structured decision-making process: (1) Perceive — identify hazards and changes in the situation, (2) Process — evaluate the risk and determine the best course of action, (3) Perform — implement the decision and monitor the outcome. This systematic approach helps prevent hasty or incomplete decisions. Use it continuously throughout the flight.

questions.question: The CARE checklist for risk mitigation stands for:-
questions.explanation: CARE helps evaluate risky decisions: Consequences (what could happen?), Alternatives (what else could I do?), Reality (am I being realistic about my abilities and the situation?), External pressures (what is influencing my decision?). If you're rationalizing a risky decision, use CARE to challenge your thinking and consider safer alternatives.

questions.question: The TEAM approach to resource management means:-

options.text: Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate (risk management strategies)

questions.explanation: TEAM describes risk management strategies: Transfer (shift risk to another party, e.g., use ATC services), Eliminate (remove the hazard entirely, e.g., cancel flight), Accept (acknowledge risk and proceed with caution), Mitigate (reduce risk, e.g., carry extra fuel, file IFR). Choose the most appropriate strategy for each identified risk.

questions.question: Single-pilot resource management (SRM) involves:-

options.text: effectively using all available resources including automation, ATC, passengers, and checklists

questions.explanation: SRM is the application of CRM principles to single-pilot operations. Resources include: automation (autopilot, GPS), ATC services, passengers (extra eyes, assistance), checklists, weather briefings, and personal knowledge/experience. Effective SRM reduces workload, improves decision-making, and enhances safety. Don't hesitate to use all available resources.

questions.question: Automation complacency occurs when:-

options.text: pilots over-rely on automated systems and fail to monitor them adequately

questions.explanation: Automation complacency is excessive trust in automated systems, leading to reduced monitoring and vigilance. Pilots may fail to detect automation errors or mode changes. Prevention: understand automation limitations, actively monitor automated systems, maintain manual flying skills, and be prepared to take over manually. Automation is a tool, not a replacement for pilot judgment.

questions.question: The 'children on board' effect refers to:-

options.text: the tendency for pilots to take fewer risks when carrying children as passengers

questions.explanation: Research shows pilots tend to make more conservative decisions when carrying children as passengers, demonstrating that external factors can positively influence risk assessment. However, pilots should apply the same conservative decision-making to all flights, regardless of who is aboard. Every passenger deserves the same level of safety consideration.

questions.question: The 'return on investment' bias in decision-making can lead pilots to:-

options.text: continue a risky flight because of money or time already invested

questions.explanation: Return on investment bias (related to sunk cost fallacy) causes pilots to continue risky flights to justify money spent on rental, fuel, or time invested in planning. Example: 'I've already paid for the rental, I might as well go.' This is dangerous thinking. The money is spent regardless — base decisions on current safety, not past investment.

questions.question: The 'duck under' syndrome refers to:-

options.text: descending below minimums on an instrument approach in an attempt to see the runway

questions.explanation: The 'duck under' syndrome is the dangerous practice of descending below approach minimums without the required visual references, hoping to see the runway. This is a major cause of controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) accidents. If you reach minimums without the required visual references, execute a missed approach immediately. Never duck under — it's illegal and potentially fatal.

questions.question: Scud running is:-

options.text: flying VFR in marginal weather conditions at low altitude below clouds

questions.explanation: Scud running is flying VFR at low altitude beneath a low cloud base, often in poor visibility. It is extremely dangerous: limited escape options, terrain/obstacle hazards, inadvertent IMC, and reduced reaction time. Scud running is a major cause of VFR-into-IMC accidents. If weather deteriorates to the point where scud running seems necessary, land immediately or file IFR if qualified.

questions.question: The 'VFR-into-IMC' scenario is dangerous because:-

options.text: VFR pilots are not trained for instrument flight and spatial disorientation is likely

questions.explanation: VFR-into-IMC is one of the most lethal scenarios in general aviation. VFR pilots lack instrument training and are highly susceptible to spatial disorientation in cloud. Statistics show most VFR pilots lose control within minutes of entering IMC. If inadvertently entering IMC: maintain aircraft control, execute a 180° turn to VMC if possible, declare an emergency, and request ATC assistance.

questions.question: The '180-degree turn' technique for escaping inadvertent IMC should be:-

options.text: practiced with an instructor and executed immediately upon entering cloud
only attempted after several minutes in cloud

questions.explanation: The 180° turn is the primary escape manoeuvre from inadvertent IMC for VFR pilots. Execute it immediately upon entering cloud, before spatial disorientation develops. Technique: shallow bank (15-20°), maintain altitude, use turn coordinator, return to VMC. Practice this with an instructor under the hood. The longer you stay in cloud, the less likely you are to survive.

questions.question: Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) accidents typically occur when:-

options.text: a fully functioning aircraft is flown into terrain, water, or obstacles with the crew unaware
pilots are fully aware of terrain

questions.explanation: CFIT occurs when an airworthy aircraft under pilot control is inadvertently flown into terrain, water, or obstacles. Contributing factors: poor visibility, loss of situational awareness, spatial disorientation, distraction, inadequate planning, or failure to follow procedures. Prevention: terrain awareness, altitude awareness, proper approach procedures, and never descending below safe altitudes without visual contact.

questions.question: The 'sterile cockpit' concept should be applied during:-

options.text: all critical phases of flight including taxi, takeoff, approach, and landing

questions.explanation: The sterile cockpit rule prohibits non-essential activities and conversations during critical phases: taxi, takeoff, climb below 10,000 ft, approach, and landing. This reduces distractions during high-workload periods. Essential communication (checklists, ATC, safety-related) is always permitted. Even in single-pilot operations, avoid non-essential tasks during critical phases.

questions.question: Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) is:-

options.text: a systematic approach to mental processes used by pilots to determine the best course of action

questions.explanation: ADM is the systematic approach to the mental process of evaluating a given set of circumstances and determining the best course of action. Good ADM involves: recognizing hazards, assessing risks, identifying alternatives, making decisions, and evaluating outcomes. ADM can be learned and improved through training and experience. It is a critical skill for all pilots.

questions.question: Risk management in aviation involves:-

options.text: identifying hazards, assessing risks, and implementing controls to reduce risk to acceptable levels

questions.explanation: Risk management is a systematic process: (1) Identify hazards, (2) Assess the risk (likelihood and severity), (3) Implement controls to mitigate risk, (4) Monitor and review. Risk cannot be eliminated entirely, but it can be reduced to acceptable levels. Effective risk management is proactive, not reactive. It should be applied throughout flight planning and execution.

questions.question: The safety management system (SMS) approach emphasizes:-

options.text: proactive hazard identification and risk management rather than reactive accident investigation
only investigating accidents after they occur

questions.explanation: SMS is a systematic, proactive approach to managing safety. Key components: safety policy, safety risk management, safety assurance, and safety promotion. SMS focuses on identifying and mitigating hazards before accidents occur, rather than just investigating accidents afterward. It promotes a just culture where reporting is encouraged and system improvements are made.

questions.question: A 'near miss' or 'close call' should be:-

options.text: reported and analyzed to prevent future incidents

questions.explanation: Near misses are valuable learning opportunities. They reveal weaknesses in the system before an accident occurs. Reporting near misses (to aviation authorities, safety reporting systems) helps identify trends and implement preventive measures. A near miss is a warning — the next time, you might not be lucky. Learn from it and share the lesson.

questions.question: The 'normalization of deviance' in aviation safety means:-

options.text: gradually accepting non-standard practices as normal when no immediate consequences occur

questions.explanation: Normalization of deviance occurs when repeated rule violations or shortcuts without immediate negative consequences lead to acceptance of the deviant behaviour as normal. Over time, the safety margin erodes until an accident occurs. Example: consistently flying with minimum fuel reserves. Prevention: maintain strict adherence to standards and procedures, regardless of past 'success' with shortcuts.

questions.question: The concept of 'safety culture' in aviation refers to:-

options.text: the shared values, beliefs, and practices regarding safety within an organization or community

questions.explanation: Safety culture is the collective commitment to safety at all levels of an organization or community. A positive safety culture values: open communication, reporting without fear, learning from errors, continuous improvement, and leadership commitment to safety. A strong safety culture reduces accidents and incidents. Every pilot contributes to aviation's safety culture.

questions.question: Continuous learning and self-improvement for pilots should include:-

options.text: regular training, reading accident reports, attending safety seminars, and seeking feedback
stopping all learning after obtaining a license

questions.explanation: Aviation is a continuous learning process. Effective pilots: maintain currency and proficiency, pursue additional ratings and training, read accident reports and safety publications, attend safety seminars, seek feedback from instructors and peers, and stay current with regulations and technology. Learning from others' mistakes is far less costly than learning from your own.

questions.question: The most important factor in aviation safety is:-

options.text: the pilot's attitude, decision-making, and commitment to safety

questions.explanation: While aircraft technology, weather, and other factors are important, the pilot's attitude, judgment, and decision-making are the most critical factors in aviation safety. Most accidents are caused by human factors, not mechanical failures. A safety-focused attitude, good ADM skills, proper training, and conservative decision-making are the foundations of safe flying.

questions.question: The primary goal of human factors training in aviation is to:-

options.text: help pilots recognize and manage human limitations to improve safety and performance

questions.explanation: Human factors training helps pilots understand human capabilities and limitations (physiological, psychological, and cognitive) and provides strategies to manage them. The goal is not to eliminate human error (impossible) but to recognize error-prone situations, implement defenses, and recover from errors before they lead to accidents. Understanding human factors makes pilots safer and more effective.
